submission.natural_language_explanation: L2/N829+ is a retrospective lexical detector: the token itself sets the strength (the same word fires after '.', 'he', 'his' or 'the'), and it fires only on a fixed, closed set of English content words from the register of personal narrative, reported stance and commitment - the stance adverbs 'surely', 'hopefully', 'presumably', 'apparently', 'luckily', 'fortunately', 'thankfully', 'maybe'; the assertive/commissive verbs 'claim', 'swear/swore/sworn', 'pledge', 'plead', 'agree', 'admit', 'testify', 'promise', 'assert', 'decide', 'presume', 'figure', 'guess', 'suppose', 'think', 'hope', 'return'; the person, kin and role nouns 'man', 'men', 'brother', 'son', 'father', 'friend(s)', 'gentleman', 'lady', 'boy', 'daughter', 'citizen', 'client', 'servant', 'neighbour', 'comrade', 'roommate', 'councillor', 'acquaintance'; the body-part nouns 'face', 'head', 'neck', 'finger', 'shoulder', 'back', 'knee', 'nose'; the obligation words 'motion', 'justice', 'duty', 'right', 'oath', 'allegiance'; and the clause linkers 'that', 'whether', 'whose', 'whom', 'without', 'once'. The class is a word list and not a semantic category, so the frequent or modern neighbours of those words stay below the pole's activity line ('woman', 'women', 'girl', 'mother', 'sister', 'hand', 'eye', 'foot', 'heart', 'said', 'spoke', 'declare', 'confess', 'deny', 'vow', 'court', 'judge', 'law', 'uncle', 'cousin', 'witness', 'hero', 'cheek', 'elbow'), paraphrasing with a synonym is predicted inactive, and there is no lookahead component (ablating the pole moves the next-token distribution by KL about 1e-8).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
In the winter of 1897 the harbour at Whitby froze solid for eleven weeks. Fishing boats lay locked in the ice like toys left out in a storm, and the crews walked inland to look for work at the mills. The town board met twice a week, argued over coal rations, and printed a notice in the local paper advising families to keep their stoves low and their windows sealed. Nobody was happy, but the notice was obeyed.

A schoolmaster named Ellery kept a diary through those weeks. He recorded the price of bread, the number of gulls still circling the pier, and the small favors exchanged between households. His entries are short, dry and often funny, and they give a clearer picture of the winter than any later history of the region. On the ninth of January he wrote about a resident who had traded a sack of turnips for a pair of boots, and he added a line about the ice singing in the night, a sound he compared to a distant choir.

The board eventually hired a crew to cut a channel through the ice. The work took six days and cost more than the town could comfortably afford. When the channel opened, two boats went out and came home with a modest catch of cod. The rest of the fleet waited for the thaw. By March the harbour was clear, the mills had reopened, and the crews who had walked inland came home to find their boats undamaged but their nets rotten.

Not everyone stayed. A dozen families took the coach road south before the worst of the weather and did not come home until spring. The houses they left stood empty, and the frost split the plaster in several of them. The board later paid a mason to patch the walls, a cost nobody had budgeted for, and the bill was still being argued over two years afterward.

Historians who have studied the episode argue about almost everything except its scale. Some argue the freeze was a turning point for the local economy; others insist it changed nothing at all, and the town would have declined anyway as the herring shoals moved north. The diary of the schoolmaster, preserved in the county archive, is the only source everyone trusts. It contains, presumably, the full account of the winter, though nobody has read every page. explanation_scores.explanation: L2/N829+ is a retrospective lexical detector: the token itself sets the strength (the same word fires after '.', 'he', 'his' or 'the'), and it fires only on a fixed, closed set of English content words from the register of personal narrative, reported stance and commitment - the stance adverbs 'surely', 'hopefully', 'presumably', 'apparently', 'luckily', 'fortunately', 'thankfully', 'maybe'; the assertive/commissive verbs 'claim', 'swear/swore/sworn', 'pledge', 'plead', 'agree', 'admit', 'testify', 'promise', 'assert', 'decide', 'presume', 'figure', 'guess', 'suppose', 'think', 'hope', 'return'; the person, kin and role nouns 'man', 'men', 'brother', 'son', 'father', 'friend(s)', 'gentleman', 'lady', 'boy', 'daughter', 'citizen', 'client', 'servant', 'neighbour', 'comrade', 'roommate', 'councillor', 'acquaintance'; the body-part nouns 'face', 'head', 'neck', 'finger', 'shoulder', 'back', 'knee', 'nose'; the obligation words 'motion', 'justice', 'duty', 'right', 'oath', 'allegiance'; and the clause linkers 'that', 'whether', 'whose', 'whom', 'without', 'once'. The class is a word list and not a semantic category, so the frequent or modern neighbours of those words stay below the pole's activity line ('woman', 'women', 'girl', 'mother', 'sister', 'hand', 'eye', 'foot', 'heart', 'said', 'spoke', 'declare', 'confess', 'deny', 'vow', 'court', 'judge', 'law', 'uncle', 'cousin', 'witness', 'hero', 'cheek', 'elbow'), paraphrasing with a synonym is predicted inactive, and there is no lookahead component (ablating the pole moves the next-token distribution by KL about 1e-8).
